Reset after a miss

A miss is over the moment the shot is fired; only the next target can still change. A short, fixed reset helps you leave the miss behind and start the next routine.

Little research

  1. Gun safe: handle it as the rules require, muzzles in a safe direction.
  2. One slow breath out.
  3. One correction in two or three words, for example “stay on the line”.
  4. A quick picture in your head of the right shot.
  5. Your next pre-shot routine.

Coaches' experience

The reset has to fit the time limit. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ you have at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles. In Compak® Sporting you have at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target.

Save the “why” for after the round. Analysing a skill step by step under pressure can disrupt it, so on the stand keep to one short correction.

Some research

Sporting™ In Sporting™ the rules ask you to check your score on the card when you leave the stand (Chapter 16 · Recording results and checking your score).

Once you know the score of a stand, let it go: that stand is closed, and your attention belongs to the next one.

Coaches' experience

The same reset works after a referee decision you dislike. If you disagree, make a protest at once and in the correct way, then let it go once the decision is final. More in Warnings, cards and penalties.

Coaches' experience

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Protest at once on the stand: raise a hand and say “appeal” or “protest” (Chapter 9 · How to protest on the stand). After the final decision you must shoot again within 15 seconds (Chapter 10 · Resume shooting within 15 seconds).

Compak® Sporting

Protest at once, before the next shooter calls: raise an arm and say “protest” or “appeal” (Chapter 19 · How to protest a referee's call). After the final decision you must resume within 10 seconds (Chapter 21 · Refusal to comply: 10 seconds to resume).

Going on arguing after a final decision counts as an attempt to influence the referee and can be penalised (Chapter 11 · What counts as influencing the referee, Chapter 22 · What counts as an attempt to influence).

A bad stand is not a bad day. Some shooters lose points early from nerves and shoot well once they settle; coaches often advise judging the day at the end, not after one stand.

Coaches' experience

Key points

  • Reset in 5–10 seconds: gun safe, breath out, one correction, one picture, next routine.
  • Ask “why” after the round, not on the stand.
  • After a referee decision: protest at once and correctly, then let it go.
  • A bad stand is not a bad day.

Did you know?

In a study of tenpin bowlers, a short routine after each throw also helped, and players felt it protected their focus.

For parents
  • When your child misses, stay calm and quiet on the side. A calm face helps more than advice, and advice from behind the stand can count as coaching.
For the interpreter
  • After a miss, do not translate comments or analysis unless the shooter asks. During a competition, pass on only the referee's decisions and official messages.
For the coach
  • In training, practise the reset on purpose: after a missed target, ask the shooter to say the five steps aloud, then do them in silence.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What is the first step of the reset after a miss?

    1. Work out exactly why you missed
    2. Count up your score for the round so far
    3. Make the gun safe, as the rules say
    Answer

    Make the gun safe, as the rules say

    Safety comes first; then one breath out, one correction, one picture and the next routine.

  2. When is a good time to analyse why you missed?

    1. After the round
    2. Before the next call
    3. During the next presentation
    Answer

    After the round

    Step-by-step analysis on the stand can disrupt your shooting; one short correction is enough there.

  3. You disagree with a referee's “zero”. What do you do?

    1. Argue until the referee agrees
    2. Protest at once, then let it go
    3. Complain to the squad after the round
    Answer

    Protest at once, then let it go

    Protest at once in the correct way; once the decision is final, arguing on counts as an attempt to influence the referee.

    Chapter 9 · How to protest on the stand
